title: How the Science of Reading Comprehension Has Led Us Astray
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler argues that scientific evidence is straightforwardly useful for decoding but misleading for comprehension, because short experiments can only measure what changes within a few weeks. Strategy instruction shows gains in studies of six weeks or less, while background knowledge and familiarity with written language take far longer to build and so go unmeasured. The result, she says, is an elementary day devoted to practising skills and strategies on disconnected passages. She traces the history from basal readers through 1970s expert-reader research and the whole-language adoption of strategies, and she questions the neat distinction between skills and strategies. A Keene anecdote and a 2009 content-focused versus strategy-focused study show that without knowledge of the topic neither technique helps. She promises a follow-up on preserving what is valuable in the evidence.
points: Phonics research is a clean case for experimentation, while comprehension is too gradual and multi-factor for short studies to capture.
Because strategies are easy to test and knowledge is not, schools over-weighted strategies and skills practice on disconnected passages.
No study endorsed teaching one strategy for weeks at a time year after year, yet people came to assume one did.
Skills and strategies share a limit: without topic knowledge and vocabulary, neither kind of technique helps a reader.
A 2009 study found content-focused discussion improved comprehension and retention more than strategy-focused lessons.
quotes: Scientific studies generally try to isolate one variable and test it on a “treatment” group and a “control” group for a period of days or weeks. That works well with something like decoding, which involves a defined set of skills that can be taught directly. Results can be seen pretty quickly.

Given the abundance of data on the effectiveness of strategies, educators and reading experts have placed greater weight on comprehension “skills and strategies” than on the other elements of comprehension. That has led to a situation where, aside from time reserved for math, the elementary school day is devoted largely to practicing skills and strategies on disconnected reading passages—with little attention paid to building kids’ knowledge or familiarity with writing conventions.

The research hadn’t been turned into anything resembling a curriculum, so teachers improvised. One influential literacy guru, Ellin Keene, interpreted the findings to mean that teachers should “model” one strategy at a time, spending weeks on each, and teaching them year after year beginning in kindergarten. No studies endorsed Keene’s approach, although eventually people assumed they did.

That anecdote illustrates one thing skills and strategies have in common: if you don’t have enough knowledge and vocabulary relating to the topic to make at least some sense of the text, neither kind of technique will help you. Let’s say Keene advised Jeremy to use the evidence-backed strategy of asking himself questions about the text as he went along. Without more knowledge of the Revolution, he wouldn’t have been able to answer them.

In the content-focused classroom, teachers asked open-ended questions like “How does all this connect with what we read earlier?” Not only did that lead to richer discussion, it also boosted students’ comprehension and retention of information compared to the kids in the strategy-focused classroom.

With the best of intentions, educators and some reading experts have looked at research that is fine as far as it goes but have drawn conclusions it doesn’t support—and that have led to devastating consequences for many children. That doesn’t mean we should dismiss the evidence on comprehension strategies—or even “skills.” There are ways to preserve the baby while throwing out the harmful bathwater.
